Estuary Fish Survey: Data Cleaning, Integration and Visualisation

Author

Kendra Sturdee

Published

November 19, 2026

Introduction

The goal of this exercise is to wrangle extremely messy data, and produce a final clean dataset and figure on the Ross River estuary fish surveys. The data are from a previous PhD student who conducted surveys over 30 days in May 2026 at four different sites along the Ross River estuary, Townsville, Queensland, Australia. The data include catch counts for four different fish species, as well as environmental data (temperature, salinity, and turbidity) collected at each site using sonde sensors.

Packages and housekeeping

#| message: true
#| warning: false

# Load required packages
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(readxl)
library(here)

Main dataset

The catch data is split across 4 tabs in one excel file Load. We must load them indivudally.

# Define the original catch-log location
catch_file <- here::here(
  "data",
  "workshop2",
  "estuary_catch_log.xlsx"
)

# Import the four worksheets
catch1 <- readxl::read_excel(catch_file, sheet = 1)
catch2 <- readxl::read_excel(catch_file, sheet = 2)
catch3 <- readxl::read_excel(catch_file, sheet = 3)
catch4 <- readxl::read_excel(catch_file, sheet = 4)

# Import site metadata
metadata <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here(
    "data",
    "workshop2",
    "estuary_metadata.csv"
  )
)

# Import the taxonomic dictionary
species_dict <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here(
    "data",
    "workshop2",
    "species_dictionary.csv"
  )
)

Sites names differ between the catch log and the metadata. The catch log has site names in the format “lower_ross”, “middle_ross”, “upper_ross”, and “upper_ross2”, while the metadata has site names in the format “Lower Ross”, “Middle Ross”, “Upper Ross”, and “Upper Ross 2”. These must be made consistent before I can join the datasets together.

Clean and standardised site names and convert character to factor variables

catch_data <- catch_data |>
  mutate(
    site = str_to_lower(str_trim(site)),
    site = str_replace_all(site, " ", "_")) |> 
  # Convert all chr to fct
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as_factor)
  )

metadata <- metadata |>
  mutate(
    site_name = str_to_lower(str_trim(site_name)),
    site_name = str_replace_all(site_name, " ", "_")) |> 
  # Convert all chr to fct
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as_factor)
  )

Load Taxonomic Dictionary

# Inspect the taxonomic dictionary
head(species_dict)

  common_name   scientific_name          
  <chr>         <chr>                    
1 barramundi    Lates calcarifer         
2 mangrove_jack Lutjanus argentimaculatus
3 bream         Acanthopagrus spp.       
4 flathead      Platycephalus spp.

Must reference common names in catch log to those in the taxonomic dictionary before we do a join.

catch_data |> 
  distinct(species)
# A tibble: 4 × 1
  species      
  <fct>        
1 barramundi   
2 MANGROVE JACK
3 bream        
4 flathead     
# Can see these are different to the dictionary
species_dict |>
  distinct(common_name)
# A tibble: 4 × 1
  common_name  
  <chr>        
1 barramundi   
2 mangrove_jack
3 bream        
4 flathead

Only difference is between mangrove_jack and MANGROVE JACK. We can fix this by standardising the species names in the catch log to match those in the dictionary.

Standardise species (common name) variable in the catch log to match dictionary

# Standardise species names in the catch log
catch_data <- catch_data |>
  mutate(
    species = as.character(species),
    species = str_to_lower(str_trim(species)),
    species = str_replace_all(species, " ", "_")
  )

# Standardise species names in the taxonomic dictionary
species_dict <- species_dict |>
  mutate(
    common_name = as.character(common_name),
    common_name = str_to_lower(str_trim(common_name)),
    common_name = str_replace_all(common_name, " ", "_")
  )

Still must create scientific_name variables

Create new variable (“scientific_name”) in catch log by joining with taxonomic dictionary

catch_data <- catch_data |>
  mutate(common_name = species) |>
  left_join(species_dict, by = join_by(common_name))

Notes on sensor data

Sensor data includes 15-minute sonde data for the same 4 sites and 30 days of sampling. The sourced script above turned this into daily data and removed outliers. There are three different environmental variables measured: temperature, salinity, and turbidity. We could investigate the effects of all three on fish species abundance or pick one… Let’s remember that the goal of this exercise is to produce a publication-ready visualisation of the estuary’s ecology.

The sensor data is now in a dataframe called sensor_daily, which has the following variables: site, date, mean_temp, mean_salinity, and mean_turbidity. We can join this with the catch data and metadata to create a final dataset for analysis.

Join catch data with metadata and sensor data

catch_data_final <- catch_data |>
  left_join(metadata, by = join_by(site == site_name)) |>
  left_join(sensor_daily, by = join_by(site, date))

At first glance it looks good. However, note that there are only 427 rows of data. This is less than the expected 480 rows (4 species x 4 sites x 30 surveys). This discrepancy is likely due to some days where there were zero counts of certain species at different sites. We need to wrangle these into a complete dataset with 480 rows, where the zero counts are explicitly represented as 0 rather than NA. This is important for our subsequent analyses and visualisations, as we want to be able to distinguish between true absences (0) and missing data (NA)

Wrangle final dataset

# Standardise zone order and complete missing species records
catch_data_final <- catch_data_final |>
  mutate(
    zone = factor(
      as.character(zone),
      levels = c(
        "Upstream",
        "Middle",
        "Downstream"
      )
    )
  ) |>
  tidyr::complete(
    tidyr::nesting(
      site,
      date,
      lat,
      lon,
      zone,
      mean_temp,
      mean_salinity,
      mean_turbidity
    ),
    scientific_name
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # Missing species records within completed surveys represent zero catches
    count = coalesce(count, 0)
  )

# Confirm the completed dataset contains 480 records
stopifnot(nrow(catch_data_final) == 480)

Perfect, we now have 480 rows. Now, we can shift gears and start thinking about how we want to analyze and interpret this data. We can start by looking at the environmental variables (salinity, turbidity, temperature) across the different zones (downstream, midstream, upstream), and then we can look at the fish abundance patterns across these zones.

Salinity

# Summarise salinity using unique site-date observations
# This avoids counting the same daily sensor measurement multiple times

sal_sum <- catch_data_final |>
  dplyr::distinct(
    site,
    date,
    zone,
    mean_salinity
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(zone) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_salinity = sum(!is.na(mean_salinity)),

    sd_salinity = sd(
      mean_salinity,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    median_salinity = median(
      mean_salinity,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    mean_salinity = mean(
      mean_salinity,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    sem_salinity = sd_salinity / sqrt(n_salinity),

    .groups = "drop"
  )

print(sal_sum)
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  zone       n_salinity sd_salinity median_salinity mean_salinity sem_salinity
  <fct>           <int>       <dbl>           <dbl>         <dbl>        <dbl>
1 Upstream           30       0.191            4.99          4.99       0.0348
2 Middle             30       0.399           15.0          14.9        0.0728
3 Downstream         30       0.354           28.0          28.0        0.0646
4 <NA>               30       0.104           34.0          34.0        0.0190
# Create a figure theme to use for all figures for consistency and professionalism
marine_theme <- theme_classic() +
theme(
text = element_text(size = 14, colour = "black"),
axis.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
axis.text = element_text(size = 12),
plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 13),
legend.title = element_text(size = 13),
legend.text = element_text(size = 12)
)

# Visualize
sal_sum |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = zone, y = median_salinity)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = median_salinity - sd_salinity, ymax = median_salinity + sd_salinity), width = 0.2) +
  marine_theme +
  labs(#title = "Median Salinity by Zone with Standard Deviation Error Bars",
       x = "Zone",
       y = "Median Salinity (ppt)")

Interpretation

There is a clear difference in salinity across the zones, with the downstream zone having the highest salinity, and the upstream zone having the lowest. This is consistent with our expectations for an estuarine system, where salinity typically decreases as you move upstream from the ocean.

Turbidity

turb_sum <- 
  catch_data_final |>
  group_by(zone) |>
  summarise(
    sd_turbidity = sd(mean_turbidity, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_turbidity = median(mean_turbidity, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_turbidity = mean(mean_turbidity, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

turb_sum |>
  ggplot(aes(x = zone, y = median_turbidity)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = median_turbidity - sd_turbidity, ymax = median_turbidity + sd_turbidity), width = 0.2) +
  marine_theme +
  labs(
       x = "Zone",
       y = "Median Turbidity (NTU)")

Interpretation

Median turbidity is highest in the midstream zone, and lowest in the downstream zone. This could be due to a number of factors, including sediment input from upstream sources, or differences in water flow and mixing across the zones. However overall, the differences in turbidity across the zones are not as pronounced as those for salinity, and the standard deviations are relatively large (range: 2.1-4.8 NTU), indicating high variability in turbidity within each zone.

Temperature

temp_sum <- 
  catch_data_final |>
  group_by(zone) |>
  summarise(
    sd_temperature = sd(mean_temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_temperature = median(mean_temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_temperature = mean(mean_temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

temp_sum |>
  ggplot(aes(x = zone, y = median_temperature)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = median_temperature - sd_temperature, ymax = median_temperature + sd_temperature), width = 0.2) +
  marine_theme +
  labs(
       x = "Zone",
       y = "Median Temperature (°C)")

Interpretation

Median temperature is highest in the upstream zone, and lowest in the downstream zone (excluding the marine zone). This is consistent with our expectations for an estuarine system, where water temperature typically increases as you move upstream from the ocean. However, the differences in temperature across the zones are not as pronounced as those for salinity, and the standard deviations are relatively large (range: 0.8-1.2 °C), indicating high variability in temperature within each zone.

Because temperature and turbidity are not as strongly differentiated across the zones as salinity, I will focus on salinity as my main environmental variable of interest in my subsequent analyses and visualisations (though I will keep in mind the differences in turbidity and temperature across the zones, which could also be influencing fish abundance patterns).

Fish abundance and summary stats

# Summarise fish catch by zone and species
fish_summary <- catch_data_final |>
  dplyr::group_by(
    zone,
    scientific_name
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_catch = sum(!is.na(count)),

    mean_catch = mean(
      count,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    sd_catch = sd(
      count,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    sem_catch = sd_catch / sqrt(n_catch),

    .groups = "drop"
  )


# Summarise salinity using unique site-date observations
salinity_summary <- catch_data_final |>
  dplyr::distinct(
    site,
    date,
    zone,
    mean_salinity
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(zone) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_salinity = sum(!is.na(mean_salinity)),

    mean_salinity = mean(
      mean_salinity,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    sd_salinity = sd(
      mean_salinity,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    sem_salinity = sd_salinity / sqrt(n_salinity),

    .groups = "drop"
  )


# Combine fish and environmental summaries
Final_stats <- fish_summary |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    salinity_summary,
    by = "zone"
  )

print(Final_stats)

Final_stats |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = zone, 
             y = mean_catch, 
             fill = scientific_name, 
             colour = scientific_name)) +
  geom_line(group = 1) +
  # add in points from master data
  geom_point(
    data = catch_data_final, 
    aes(x = zone, 
        y = count, 
        colour = scientific_name),
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.2), 
    alpha = 0.4, 
    size = 1.5, 
    inherit.aes = FALSE) + 
  geom_point(
    position = "dodge", 
    size = 5, 
    pch = 23,
    colour = "black") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = earth_cols) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = earth_cols_dark) +
  # SE pretty narrow, potentially not worth plotting but let's viewer see that included
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_catch - sem_catch, ymax = mean_catch + sem_catch), 
                position = position_dodge(0.9), width = 0.2) + 
  facet_wrap(~ scientific_name, scales = "fixed") +
  marine_theme +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "italic", size = 12, colour = "black"), # spp names in italic
   # legend.position = "bottom"
    legend.position = "none" # legend unnecessary
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Spatial Zone",
    # scientific label for y axis of n day -1 use regex to get superscript
    y = "Abundance (per day)"
  )
